That's the year Rabbi Mordechai Avraham Shor and his son founded what's considered the first commercial, modern winery in the region, inspired by philanthropist Sir Moses Montefiore's encouragement to replant vines in the Holy Land.

How many generations has the family been making wine?
Eight, as of the founding of the modern 1848 Winery brand in 2006 by Yossi Shor, who wanted to honour that 1848 founding date directly in the name.

Yes — 1848 Winery produces kosher-certified wines as part of its identity, reflecting its Jerusalem roots.

Why is it called ""One Source""?
All the wheat and water used to make Absolut comes from the Åhus area of southern Sweden, and every step from growing the grain to bottling happens in one place — the company's own term for this is ""One Source.""

What makes continuous distillation different?
Founder Lars Olsson Smith introduced it to Sweden in 1879, distilling the spirit far more times than the standard three or four pot-still passes used elsewhere at the time, for a purer, more consistent result.

Why is there a man's portrait on the bottle?
That's Lars Olsson Smith himself, nicknamed ""the Vodka King"" in Sweden — his medallion has appeared on every bottle since the brand's earliest days.

How do I make a Paper Plane?
Equal parts — 22.5ml each of Amaro Nonino, bourbon, Aperol and fresh lemon juice. Shake hard with ice and strain into a coupe. No garnish needed. It is one of the few modern cocktails to have entered the canon outright, and this bottle is the non-negotiable part of it.

Is it very bitter?
Far less than you would expect. The grappa base and barrique ageing make it noticeably sweeter, rounder and more orange-forward than most amari — which is exactly why it is the one bartenders reach for when introducing someone to the category.

Anyone who has got into cocktails in the last couple of years, anyone who loves Italy, and anyone who already owns the obvious bottles. The wax-sealed bottle looks expensive on a bar cart, and it is a name that signals you knew what you were choosing.

Is it actually hot?
Warm rather than hot. Ancho chillies are poblanos that have been ripened and dried, which trades sharp capsaicin heat for raisin, tobacco and smoke. You get a gentle glow at the back of the throat, well behind the fruit and spice.

What does it taste like?
Dried chilli and raisin first, then cinnamon, cacao and a faint smokiness, finishing with lingering warmth rather than burn. It is closer to a spiced fruit liqueur than to anything you would call spicy.

What is the easiest thing to make with it?
Ancho Reyes and ginger beer over ice with a lime wedge — two ingredients, thirty seconds, and it tastes like something a bar made. After that, put a measure into a Margarita and you have the spicy Margarita everyone orders out.

Who is this a good gift for?
The person who has the tequila and the mezcal and is looking for the next thing, and anyone who cooks with chillies. It is a genuinely unusual bottle to receive — most people have never been given a chilli liqueur, and almost everyone likes it.

What is the difference between cachaça and rum?
Most rum is made from molasses, a by-product of sugar refining. Cachaça must be made from fresh-pressed sugarcane juice, and only in Brazil. That gives it a greener, grassier, more vegetal character — closer to rhum agricole than to a Caribbean dark rum.

What does amburana wood taste like?
Unmistakable. Amburana is a native Brazilian hardwood that gives an intense cinnamon-and-vanilla sweetness with a hint of caraway — a flavour no oak cask can produce. It is the single most distinctive thing about this bottle, and the reason bartenders seek it out.

Does it make a better caipirinha?
Considerably. Most caipirinhas are made with cheap industrial cachaça, which is why they taste of little but lime and sugar. Swap in an aged single-estate bottling and the drink gains warmth, spice and length — and it is why the passionfruit caipirinha has taken off this year.

Who is this a good gift for?
Someone who makes cocktails and has never owned a proper cachaça, or anyone who loves Brazil. It is an unusual bottle in the best sense — nobody else will have given it, and the flavour is genuinely unlike anything else on the shelf.

What exactly is pisco?
A grape brandy from Peru, distilled from wine and bottled without ageing. Where cognac and armagnac spend years in oak, pisco is rested in neutral vessels so the character of the grape survives intact. It is closer in spirit to a great eau de vie than to a brandy.

Why does ""never diluted"" matter?
Almost every other spirit is distilled strong and then watered down to bottling strength. Peruvian law forbids it — the distiller has to land the cut exactly at drinking strength. It is far harder to do and it leaves noticeably more texture and aroma in the glass.

How do I make a proper Pisco Sour?
50ml pisco, 25ml fresh lime juice, 20ml sugar syrup and one fresh egg white. Dry-shake without ice first to build the foam, then shake hard with ice and strain into a coupe. Three drops of Angostura on the foam to finish. It is one of the great sours, and Quebranta is the grape it was designed around.

Who is this a good gift for?
Anyone building a serious cocktail cabinet who has covered gin, rum and whisky but not yet pisco — and anyone who loves Peruvian food. It is an unusual bottle to receive, which is exactly what makes it land.

What does D.O.M. stand for?
Deo Optimo Maximo — ""to God, most good, most great"" — the traditional Benedictine dedication. It has been on the label since Alexandre Le Grand began bottling in 1863, and it is not a strength or an age statement, which is the usual guess.

How is it different from other herbal liqueurs?
It is the sweet, honeyed one. Where Chartreuse is bracing and Jägermeister is dark and bitter, Bénédictine leads with honey and saffron, with the herbs sitting underneath. If someone has found herbal liqueurs too punishing, this is the one that changes their mind.

Is the monastery story true?
Partly, and the house is relaxed about it. There was a Benedictine abbey at Fécamp, and monks there did distil. Whether Le Grand genuinely found a 1510 recipe in his family papers or built a very good story around his own formula is something historians still enjoy arguing about.

How is Madeira different from port or sherry?
All three are fortified, but Madeira is the only one deliberately heated and oxidised during ageing. That process gives it a piercing acidity none of the others have — which is why a sweet Madeira never tastes cloying, and why it survives being open almost indefinitely.

What does Malmsey mean?
It is the English name for Malvasia, the richest of Madeira's four noble grapes. The scale runs Sercial (bone dry), Verdelho, Bual, then Malmsey (sweetest). Malmsey is the one to start with — it is the most immediately generous and the easiest to love.

Does it really keep once opened?
Yes, genuinely. Because the wine has already been through heat and oxidation, air does very little to it. Recorked and kept somewhere cool, a bottle will drink well for a year or more. It is the ideal bottle for someone who wants one glass on a Sunday, not a whole bottle in a night.

Who is this a good gift for?
Anyone who likes port but has never explored Madeira, and anyone with a cheeseboard habit. The half-bottle size makes it an elegant addition to a hamper, and the fact that it keeps means it never feels like a burden to open.

Is this too smoky for someone new to Islay?
No — and that is precisely why it won. Twenty-one years and a Pedro Ximénez finish round the peat into something closer to woodsmoke over dried fruit than the medicinal punch of a young Islay. It is the bottle to convert someone with, not the one to frighten them with.

What does the Pedro Ximénez finish actually add?
PX is the sweetest, darkest sherry there is. A final rest in first-fill PX casks lays raisin, fig and dark chocolate over the whisky, giving it a viscous, almost dessert-like weight that carries the smoke rather than being buried by it.

Should I keep it or open it?
Open it. Whisky does not improve in the bottle, and a World's Best Single Malt is a poor thing to admire through glass. If it is a gift for a collector, the presentation box shows well on a shelf either way.

Why is a 21-year-old Islay so much more expensive?
Roughly two per cent of each cask evaporates every year. After twenty-one years a meaningful share of the original spirit is simply gone, and the casks that survive that long in good condition are a small minority. You are paying for time and for attrition.

Does vermouth need refrigerating once opened?
Yes. Vermouth is wine-based, so once the seal is broken it oxidises like wine. Keep it in the fridge and it will stay in good condition for around a month or two. A bottle left open on a warm shelf for a year is the reason so many people think they dislike vermouth.

How is this different from ordinary sweet vermouth?
Concentration. Antica Formula is markedly richer, more spiced and more bitter-edged than a standard rosso, with a pronounced vanilla character. It is closer to an amaro in weight. That is why bartenders reach for it when a drink needs backbone.

Why a litre bottle?
It is the bar format, and it is the better value. If someone is making Manhattans and Negronis with any regularity, the 75cl runs out quickly. Refrigerated, a litre keeps perfectly well.

Anyone who makes cocktails at home and has not yet upgraded their vermouth — which is most people. It is the single change that improves a home Manhattan most, and the apothecary bottle looks the part on a bar cart.

How is Armagnac different from cognac?
Two things. Armagnac is usually distilled once rather than twice, which leaves far more of the grape's character in the spirit, and it comes from Gascony rather than Charente. The result is rounder, more rustic and more obviously fruity — where cognac is elegant, Armagnac has depth.

What does XO mean here?
It guarantees the youngest spirit in the blend has spent at least ten years in oak. In practice this bottling is significantly older than the minimum, which is why it shows the dried-fruit and rancio character that only comes with real age.

<details><summary>What is ""rancio""?</summary><div class=""dh-faq-a"">A prized note in old brandies — nutty, faintly savoury, somewhere between walnut and old leather. It cannot be manufactured or rushed

Is it really that bitter?
Yes. Fernet-Branca is one of the most bitter things sold in a bottle, and it makes no apology for it — menthol, myrrh and bitter root, with almost no sugar to cushion it. Served ice cold in a small glass it becomes bracing rather than punishing, which is the trick.

What is a fernet, exactly?
A style of Italian amaro: very bitter, low in sugar, built on herbs and roots rather than fruit, and traditionally drunk as a digestivo. Fernet-Branca is the original and by far the best known — the style is effectively named after it.

Why do bartenders drink it?
Partly because it genuinely helps after a long shift and a lot of tasting, partly as a shared code. Ordering a shot of Fernet in a bar staffed by people who know it is the closest the trade has to a secret handshake.

Who is this a good gift for?
Anyone who works behind a bar, anyone who already loves amari, and the person who claims nothing is too bitter for them. Be warned: it is a strong opinion in a bottle, so give it to someone who enjoys those.

What does ""tahona-crushed"" mean?
After the agave is slow-cooked in a stone oven, it's crushed by a two-ton volcanic stone called a tahona rather than a modern roller mill — a technique nearly abandoned across the tequila industry until Fortaleza revived it.

Is Fortaleza connected to Sauza Tequila?
Yes — founder Guillermo Erickson Sauza is a direct descendant of Don Cenobio Sauza, who founded the original Sauza Tequila brand in 1873. The Sauza family sold that brand in 1976 but kept the historic La Fortaleza distillery, which Guillermo revived in 1999.

Why no barrel ageing for the Blanco?
Blanco tequila is bottled shortly after distillation specifically to preserve the raw, unfiltered character of the agave itself, rather than letting oak influence the flavour the way Reposado or Añejo styles do.

Is this a pear liqueur?
No — and the difference matters. A liqueur is sweetened and usually much lower in strength. An eau-de-vie is a distilled fruit spirit with nothing added: no sugar, no colour, no oak. It smells intensely of pear and then finishes completely dry, which catches most people out the first time.

Why is it clear?

Is this sweet?
No — the opposite. Seco means dry, and Alfonso is completely dry. The confusion is understandable: most sherry sold in Britain for decades was sweetened cream sherry, which is a different product entirely. A dry oloroso is closer in spirit to a serious white wine than to anything sugary.

What is the difference between fino and oloroso?
Flor. Fino is fortified lightly, so a living yeast cap survives on the surface and shields the wine from air — keeping it pale and delicate. Oloroso is fortified harder, the flor dies, and the wine ages in contact with oxygen instead. That is what makes it dark, nutty and full-bodied.

How long does it keep once opened?
Because it has already aged oxidatively, it is far more robust than a fino. Recorked and kept somewhere cool it will hold up well for a month or more — much longer than an ordinary white wine.

Why is Chartreuse so hard to buy?
Because the Carthusian order decided not to grow. Faced with demand rising far beyond what they had ever made, the monks chose to cap production in order to protect their contemplative life rather than build a bigger distillery. Retailers now receive small allocations, and bottles move quickly.

What is the difference between Green and Yellow?
Green is the original: 55% ABV, intensely herbal, with real heat and a long menthol finish. Yellow is gentler at 40%, sweeter and more honeyed. If you are buying for a cocktail maker, Green is the one they want.

How do I make a Last Word?
Equal parts — 22.5ml each of gin, Green Chartreuse, maraschino liqueur and fresh lime juice. Shake hard with ice and strain into a coupe. It is a Prohibition-era drink that came back from obscurity, and it is the reason so many people go looking for this bottle.

Does it really age in the bottle?
Yes — almost uniquely among spirits. Sealed bottles continue to develop for decades, softening and deepening, which is why aged bottles are collected and traded. Store it upright, away from light.

What does ""pure single rum"" actually mean?
It is the rum world's equivalent of single malt: 100% pot-still rum from one distillery, with no column-still spirit blended in and nothing added afterwards. Very few estates anywhere still make rum this way — Hampden is the most famous of them.

What is Jamaican ""funk""?
The nickname for the intense, fruity, almost solvent-like aroma created by long wild fermentation and high ester counts. In Hampden it reads as pineapple, overripe banana and tropical blossom. It is the most distinctive flavour in rum, and the reason this distillery has a cult following.

Only three years old — is that young?
Not in the tropics. Jamaican heat drives evaporation and extraction several times faster than a Scottish warehouse, so three tropical years deliver a depth of colour and oak you would expect from a far older cool-climate spirit.

Is the charitable donation real?
Yes — £6 from every bottle sold during 2026 goes to relief efforts supporting Jamaica's recovery from storm Melissa. It is one of the rare bottles where the story on the label continues after you buy it.

What actually is a sloe?
The fruit of the blackthorn — a small, intensely sharp wild plum that grows in British hedgerows. Raw it is almost inedible. Steeped in gin with sugar for a few months it becomes something else entirely: deep, fruity and faintly almond-scented from the stones.

Is sloe gin still gin?
It is a gin liqueur — real gin with real fruit steeped in it, bottled at a lower strength. What separates the good from the poor is whether the maker used actual sloes and a proper gin base, or flavouring and neutral spirit. This is the former.

When is the right time to drink it?
Traditionally from the first cold weather onwards — shooting season, bonfire night, cold walks, Christmas. It is the one bottle that genuinely tastes better outdoors in October than indoors in June.

Who is this a good gift for?
Anyone who likes the outdoors, the gin drinker who has run out of new London Drys to try, and the host heading into autumn. At 26% it is gentle enough to be poured generously, which is rather the point.

One part to five parts cold water

I don't like aniseed — is this still worth trying?
Quite possibly. Anise is the frame here, not the whole picture. With sixty-five botanicals the dominant impression is herbal and spiced — thyme, cardamom, pepper — rather than the flat liquorice hit most people remember from cheap pastis.

Why does it go cloudy?
It is called the louche. The essential oils from anise are soluble in alcohol but not in water, so adding water throws them out of solution and the drink turns opaque gold. It is a sign the oils are real, not added flavouring.

How much water should I add?
Five parts cold water to one part pastis is the Provençal standard. Add the water to the pastis, not the other way round, and skip the ice — it mutes the herbs. Chill the water instead.

Who is this a good gift for?
Anyone who holidays in the south of France, any cook who makes fish stew, and the drinker who has worked through gin and amaro and wants the next herbal thing. It is also a genuinely striking bottle for the price.

What is shochu, and how is it different from sake?
Sake is brewed, like beer. Shochu is distilled, like whisky — usually from barley, sweet potato or rice, using the same kōji culture. It is the everyday spirit of southern Japan and outsells sake there comfortably.

Why is this one 43% when most shochu is 25%?
Because it was designed for bars outside Japan. At 25% shochu disappears behind ice and citrus. Saiten was bottled far higher so bartenders could build proper cocktails with it — and it works neat too.

Does it taste like whisky?
Not really. Both start from barley, but shochu is distilled once and never aged in oak, so what you get is the grain itself — toasted, clean, faintly banana-like — with none of the vanilla and caramel oak brings.

Who is this a good gift for?
The Japanophile, the bartender, and the drinker who has run out of new categories. Almost nobody in Britain owns a bottle of shochu, which makes it a genuinely surprising gift rather than a familiar one.

Off-dry rather than sweet. There is some natural residual sugar, but the Mosel's razor acidity balances it so completely that the wine finishes fresh, not sugary — the sweetness reads as ripe fruit.

Is absinthe legal, and is it hallucinogenic?
Entirely legal, and no. The thujone scare that drove the ban was never supported by the evidence — modern analysis of pre-ban bottles found levels far lower than the myth claimed. What made absinthe potent was simply that it is very strong spirit, and it was drunk in quantity. Diluted properly it lands around the strength of wine.

What is the louche?
As iced water is added, the essential oils fall out of solution and the spirit clouds from clear green to milky opalescent. It is not a trick — it is the physical proof that the herbs were distilled in rather than flavoured on. Watching it happen is half the pleasure.

What is the difference between cachaça and rum?
Most rum is made from molasses, a by-product of sugar refining. Cachaça must be made from fresh-pressed sugarcane juice, and only in Brazil. That gives it a greener, grassier character — closer to rhum agricole than to a Caribbean dark rum.

Why cognac casks?
A short rest in used XO cognac barrels softens the edges of a young cane spirit without turning it into an aged spirit. You get roundness and a faint vanilla lift while keeping the fresh green cane character that makes cachaça worth drinking.

Does it really improve a caipirinha?
Considerably. Most caipirinhas are made with industrial cachaça, which is why they taste of lime and sugar and little else. A properly made one gains texture, floral lift and length — it stops being a holiday drink and becomes a serious one.

What is aquavit?
Scandinavia's national spirit — a grain or potato base flavoured principally with caraway or dill, plus supporting botanicals. Think of it as gin's savoury cousin: same idea, entirely different direction. Linie is the aged, golden style rather than the clear one.

Does the sea voyage actually change it?
It does. Constant motion keeps the liquid working against the wood far more than a still warehouse cask, and the swing from tropical heat to North Sea cold pushes it in and out of the staves. The result is rounder and more integrated than land-aged aquavit of the same age.

Why is it called ""Double Cask"" if both are sherry casks?
It refers to the two different types of oak, American and European, rather than two different sherry styles. Macallan seasons both with sherry itself, then blends the resulting whiskies for a wider flavour range than either cask alone could give.

Is any bourbon cask used in this whisky?
No — unlike many ""sherry finished"" whiskies elsewhere in the industry that start in ex-bourbon barrels, Macallan's Double Cask uses casks seasoned exclusively with sherry from the outset, for both the American and European oak.

Why does Macallan's colour vary naturally?
No colouring is added to Macallan whiskies — the golden-to-amber hue comes entirely from the interaction between the spirit and the cask wood during maturation.

Why is it called a ""Super Tuscan"" rather than Chianti?
Because it includes non-traditional grapes like Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc alongside Sangiovese, Italian wine law at the time didn't allow it to carry the Chianti Classico name — so it was released under the simpler Toscana designation instead, a workaround that effectively created a new category of Italian wine.

What makes the 2021 vintage significant?
It marks Tignanello's 50th anniversary since the first 1971 release, and Antinori's own head winemaker Renzo Cotarella has called it one of his best vintages in a long career.

How long can this wine age?
With proper storage, critics expect it to continue developing well into the 2030s — it's built for long-term cellaring as much as drinking now.

What exactly is umeshu?
Japan's traditional plum liqueur, made by steeping whole green ume fruit with sugar. It is the drink Japanese families make at home each summer, and it sits somewhere between a dessert wine and a fruit liqueur — sweet, sharp and very easy to drink.

Is ume actually a plum?
Botanically it is closer to an apricot, which is why the flavour is not what a British drinker expects from ""plum wine"". Think sharp apricot with an almond-kernel edge rather than dark stewed plum.

What does the whisky add?
Depth. The Kurayoshi whisky blend goes in at the end of maceration and puts oak, vanilla and a little weight underneath the fruit — which stops it reading as simply sweet and gives it a proper finish.

Who is this a good gift for?
Anyone who loves Japan, anyone who finds spirits too strong, and any whisky drinker curious about what else Japan makes. At 14% it is also one of the easiest bottles to open on the night it arrives.

What are the three coffee beans for?
The serve is called con la mosca — ""with the fly"". Three beans float on the surface, one each for health, happiness and prosperity. Two or four is considered unlucky. Chew them as you finish the glass.

Why does it go cloudy with water?
The same reason pastis and ouzo do. Anise oils dissolve in alcohol but not in water, so adding ice or a splash drops them out of solution as a fine emulsion. It is called the louche, and it is a sign the anise is real rather than added as essence.

What makes this a sambuca rather than just an anise liqueur?
Italian law: a sambuca must be built on anethole from anise, sweetened to at least 350 grams of sugar a litre, and bottled at no less than 38%. Meletti hits all three, and adds elderflower — the sambucus the category takes its name from.

Who is this a good gift for?
The host who cooks Italian, the person who always suggests one more coffee, and anyone who enjoys a drink that comes with instructions. It is a bottle that gets opened at the table rather than put on a shelf.

Why is Michter's so hard to find?
Because the production choices deliberately limit output — low barrel entry proof yields fewer bottles per barrel, batches are small, and nothing is released to hit a date. Demand has grown faster than supply, so allocations are common and shelves empty quickly.

What does ""small batch"" mean here?
A modest number of barrels selected and married together, rather than hundreds blended for consistency at scale. It means more character in the glass — and slight, welcome variation between batches.

Bourbon or Scotch drinker — who is this for?
Both. It is rich and sweet enough to delight a committed bourbon drinker, and structured enough that a Scotch drinker will take it seriously. If you are buying for someone whose taste you do not know precisely, this is a safe and impressive choice.

Is it good in cocktails or should it be saved for sipping?
Both, honestly. It sips beautifully neat or over a large cube, and it makes possibly the best Old Fashioned you will pour at home. Bartenders reach for it precisely because it does not disappear behind sugar and bitters.

What does Nc'nean actually mean?
It is short for Neachneohain — the Gaelic ""Queen of Spirits"", a figure from Scottish legend who protected nature and went her own way. The distillery took both the name and the attitude, and built something the industry assumed was impossible.

Does organic really change how it tastes?
The bigger influences here are the long fermentation, the mixed yeasts and the red wine casks — those are what give the lemon curd and poached-peach character. Organic barley is a choice about how it is farmed rather than a flavour claim, and the distillery is refreshingly straight about that.

What does ""net zero"" mean for a distillery?
Nc'nean runs on renewable energy with a biomass boiler burning locally sourced wood chip, and has been verified net zero in its own operations since it started producing. The bottle is 100% recycled glass. No other Scotch distillery started out that way.

Will it make me hallucinate?
No. The thujone-in-wormwood scare that drove the bans has not survived scientific scrutiny — the quantities involved are far too small to have any such effect. What absinthe will do is get you drunk, because it is 68% alcohol. That is the whole of the mystery.

How do I prepare it properly?
Pour a measure into a glass, rest a slotted spoon with a sugar cube across the rim, and drip iced water over the cube — slowly, about five parts water to one of absinthe. The spirit clouds from clear green to pale opal as the oils come out of solution. That clouding is the louche, and it is the point.

Should I set fire to it?
Please do not. The flaming sugar cube is a Czech invention from the 1990s with no historical basis, and at 68% you are lighting a fire on your table for no gain. It also scorches the botanicals you have paid for.

Who is this a good gift for?
Someone with a taste for ritual. Absinthe is one of the few spirits that asks you to do something before you drink it, and the transformation in the glass is genuinely lovely to watch. Good for cocktail makers, and for anyone drawn to the Belle Époque.

What actually is Pimm's?
A fruit cup: a gin base flavoured with a secret blend of herbs, liqueurs and caramelised orange, bottled at 25% so it can be mixed long. It was designed from the start to be diluted rather than drunk neat.

What is the correct ratio?
One part Pimm's to three parts lemonade is the house standard. Some prefer one to two for a stronger jug. Fill with ice first, pour the Pimm's, then the lemonade, then the fruit — in that order, so nothing bruises.

What goes in it?
Cucumber is non-negotiable. Then strawberry, orange slices and a generous handful of mint. Apple and lemon work too. Anything more than that and you are making a fruit salad.

Who is this a good gift for?
The host, the person with a garden, and anyone throwing a party. It is the least intimidating bottle in the shop — nobody has to know anything about it to enjoy it, which is precisely why it has lasted since 1840.

Can you deliver it directly to the person I'm gifting?
Yes — enter their address at checkout and add your message. In London it can be at their door within 30–45 minutes, any hour of the day. The recipient must be 18+ with ID for our Challenge 21 check.

What does ""single pot still"" actually mean?
It is a uniquely Irish style: a mash of both malted and unmalted barley, distilled in copper pot stills at a single distillery. The raw barley is what gives it that thick, oily, slightly spicy texture you won't find in a single malt.

How is it different from ordinary Irish whiskey?
Most Irish whiskey on the shelf is a blend, softened with light grain spirit. This is the undiluted style — richer, weightier and far more characterful, matured for twelve years in sherry and bourbon wood.

Is it a good bottle for a Scotch drinker?
Very. Anyone who enjoys sherried Speyside whisky will recognise the dried fruit and spice immediately, then notice the extra oiliness that pot still brings. It converts sceptics faster than almost any other Irish bottle.

Who is this a good gift for?
The whiskey drinker who already owns the obvious bottles. It is widely regarded as the benchmark of its category, so it lands as a knowledgeable choice rather than a safe one — and it works equally well for a milestone birthday, a thank-you or a Christmas gift.

Is this really Emma Watson's gin?
Yes. Renais was founded in 2023 by Emma Watson and her brother Alex, built around their family's vineyards in Chablis. They are hands-on founders, not licensed names — Emma has been closely involved in the liquid, the bottle design and the brand from the start.

How is a grape-based gin different?
Most gin uses a neutral grain base. A grape base carries more texture and a subtle vinous softness, so the botanicals sit on something rounder. It is why Renais tastes gentler and more perfumed than a classic London Dry.

Will a traditional gin drinker like it?
Yes, though it is a different proposition to a juniper-forward London Dry. Think of it as the gin equivalent of a fine white wine — elegant, mineral and floral. It converts people who thought gin was not for them.

How is rhum agricole different from ordinary rum?
Most rum is distilled from molasses, a by-product of sugar refining. Agricole is distilled from fresh sugarcane juice, pressed and fermented within hours of the cut. The difference is immediate — grassy, mineral and vegetal where molasses rum is sweet and rounded.

What does VSOP mean here?
Under the Martinique appellation it indicates a minimum of four years in oak. Because those years are spent in tropical heat, the spirit develops far faster than it would in a cool climate — this drinks much older than four.

Will a rum drinker like it, or is it too different?
It is genuinely different, which is the point. Anyone who has worked their way through Caribbean and Latin rums and wants something new will find this the most interesting bottle in the category — and it converts whisky drinkers surprisingly often.

Who is this a good gift for?
The rum enthusiast who owns too many rums, and the serious home bartender — a ti' punch made with this is one of the great short drinks, and almost nobody in Britain has one at home. It is a knowledgeable gift rather than an obvious one.

What does ""5 Puttonyos"" mean?
A puttony is the traditional basket used to carry botrytised aszú berries. The number tells you how many baskets of that concentrated paste went into each barrel of base wine — so five puttonyos is a richer, sweeter wine than three, and closer in intensity to the very top bottlings.

Is it too sweet to drink?
No, and this is the thing people are always surprised by. Botrytis concentrates acidity at the same time as sugar, so the wine finishes bright and clean rather than syrupy. It is one of the very few dessert wines you can drink a full glass of.

How long will it keep unopened?
Decades. The combination of high sugar and high acidity makes Tokaji Aszú one of the longest-lived wines in the world — bottles from the nineteenth century are still drinking. It will not go anywhere in your cellar.

Who is this a good gift for?
A wine lover, a keen cook, or anyone marking a birth year or anniversary — Tokaji is vintage-dated and ages for decades, so it is an unusually meaningful bottle to lay down. It also happens to be one of the great sweet-wine bargains.

Why is Ruinart called the ""oldest champagne house""?
Founded in 1729 by Nicolas Ruinart, inspired by his uncle Dom Thierry Ruinart — it was the first house to produce and sell champagne as a standalone product, rather than as a byproduct of still wine production.

What are the crayères?
Ruinart's historic chalk cellars beneath Reims, originally carved as Roman quarries. They're now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and where every bottle ages for 2–3 years at a naturally stable temperature.

What does ""Blanc de Blancs"" mean?

What is singani?
Bolivia's national spirit: a brandy distilled from Muscat of Alexandria grapes grown high in the Andes. It has a protected denomination of origin, so only Bolivian production from those altitudes may use the name.

How is it different from pisco?
Both are unaged grape spirits, but singani uses only Muscat of Alexandria and only from high-altitude Bolivian vineyards. The result is markedly more floral and softer on the palate — orange blossom and white peach rather than the sharper, more herbal edge of many piscos.

What is the Soderbergh connection?
The filmmaker discovered singani while shooting in Bolivia in 2007, could not buy it back home, and spent years importing it himself. The 63 in the name is his birth year. It is now stocked by cocktail bars that had never heard of the category.

Who is this a good gift for?
The drinker who owns every gin and has run out of new things to try, the cocktail obsessive, and the film buff who will appreciate the backstory. It is genuinely unusual on a UK shelf, which is most of the pleasure of giving it.

How do I make a proper Hugo Spritz?
Fill a large wine glass with ice. Add 25ml St-Germain, top with 90ml prosecco and a splash of soda, then add a generous sprig of fresh mint and a squeeze of lime. Stir once, gently. That is the whole recipe — and it is the reason this bottle is everywhere this summer.

Is it only for spritzes?
Not at all. A small splash lifts a glass of champagne, softens a gin and tonic, and makes an excellent Elderflower Martini or French Gimlet. It is the most versatile bottle you can add to a home bar.

How long does it keep once opened?
Because the floral character is delicate, it is best kept refrigerated after opening and enjoyed within a few months — it will not spoil, but the fresh blossom notes fade over time. Realistically, a bottle rarely lasts that long.

Almost anyone. At 20% it is gentle and approachable, the bottle is beautiful, and the Hugo Spritz has made it the drink everyone wants to be able to pour at home. It is an ideal host gift, and pairs perfectly with a bottle of fizz.

What does gentian taste like?
Bitter, earthy and faintly floral — closer to a root vegetable than to citrus or herbs. It is the bitterness behind many amari and aperitifs, but here it is the whole point rather than one voice in a chorus.

How bitter is it really?
Assertively, but not aggressively. There is honeyed sweetness and orange peel underneath, and at 20% it is gentle enough to drink before a meal. Anyone who enjoys a Negroni or a grapefruit IPA will be on familiar ground.

What is a White Negroni?
Equal parts gin, Suze and a blanc vermouth, stirred over ice with a lemon twist. Invented in the 2000s and now on menus worldwide — it is the single best reason to keep a bottle of this at home.

Who is this a good gift for?
The home bartender missing one bottle, the Francophile, and anyone who has developed a taste for bitter drinks. The yellow bottle is instantly recognisable and looks striking on a shelf.

Can you deliver it directly to the person I'm gifting?
Yes — enter their address at checkout and add your message. In London it can be at their door within 30–45 minutes, any hour of the day. The recipient must be 18+ with ID for our Challenge 21 check.

Why is Cristal in a clear bottle?
Because Tsar Alexander II asked for one. He wanted to see what he was drinking, and he wanted a flat-bottomed bottle with no deep punt in which anything could be concealed. Clear glass lets light in, which champagne hates, so the bottle has been wrapped in gold cellophane ever since to keep it out.

Is there a non-vintage Cristal?
No. Cristal is only ever released as a vintage, and only in years the house judges worthy of it. In a year that falls short, no Cristal is made at all — which is why the year on the label carries real weight.

Why a pearl spoon rather than silver?
Metal reacts with the roe and leaves a faint tinny taste. Mother of pearl, bone and horn are inert, which is why caviar has never traditionally been served with a silver spoon. One is included in the box.

How should the caviar be kept before serving?
Straight into the coldest part of the fridge, around 0–4°C, and left unopened until you are ready. Serve the tin nested in ice, and finish it the same day once opened.

Isn’t sherry sweet?
Both sherries here are bone dry. Cream sherry gave the category its sweet reputation, but oloroso seco and palo cortado are dry, savoury wines — closer in spirit to a fine white burgundy than to anything sugary.

How long does sherry keep once opened?
Oloroso and palo cortado are oxidatively aged, so they are far more robust than most wine — recork and refrigerate, and they will hold for several weeks. Fino and manzanilla are the ones to drink quickly.

What is palo cortado?
A rare accident of the cellar: a wine that begins ageing under flor like an amontillado, then loses it and continues oxidatively like an oloroso. The result has the aroma of one and the body of the other. Very little is ever declared.

Should the Tondonia be decanted?
Yes — half an hour, poured carefully off any sediment. Serve at 16–18°C. It arrives ready to drink but will hold and develop for another decade.

Malbec was brought to Mendoza by a French agronomist in 1868, who saw potential in the region's high-altitude, sun-drenched terroir the grape never quite found back in Bordeaux. Mendoza now produces over 70% of Argentina's wine.

Why is the wine named for winds?
Three distinct winds shape Mendoza's vineyards: the cold Polar from the south, the warming Zonda descending from the Andes, and the Sudestada bringing freshness from the Atlantic — together they give the region its distinctive climate for growing Malbec.

How did Malbec become Argentina's signature grape?
It originated in Bordeaux, France, but was brought to Mendoza by a French agronomist in 1868. The region's high altitude and abundant sunshine suited the variety far better than its temperamental homeland climate, and it's now considered Argentina's calling card.

What does ""lightly oaked"" mean here?
Only a portion of the wine ages in French and American oak for several months, just enough to add structure and spice while letting the ripe, dark fruit character stay the main focus.

What is the difference between rye and bourbon?
Bourbon is at least 51% corn, which makes it sweet and round. Rye is at least 51% rye grain — this one is 100% — which makes it drier, spicier and more peppery. If you find bourbon a touch sweet, rye is the whiskey you have been looking for.

Is this a sipping whiskey or a cocktail whiskey?
Genuinely both, which is unusual at this age. Ten years of oak give it enough roundness to drink neat, and 100 proof gives it enough backbone that it does not vanish under vermouth and bitters. Most owners do both from the same bottle.

Why is 100% rye harder to make?
Rye is a difficult grain to work with — it foams heavily in the mash and is far less forgiving than corn. Most producers blend in corn or wheat to make life easier. Going all-rye and then ageing it a decade leaves nowhere for a flaw to hide.

Who is this a good gift for?
Anyone who makes cocktails at home, and anyone who already has the obvious bourbons. It arrives in its own presentation box, and it is the bottle that tends to get talked about when it appears on a bar cart.

Why is English whisky suddenly such a big deal?
England has gone from almost no whisky distilleries to a genuine movement in under two decades — and in 2026 an English single malt was named Whisky of the Year in a blind tasting against the world's most established distilleries. Early bottlings from breakout English distilleries are exactly the ones collectors later wish they had bought.

What does ""lightly peated"" actually taste like?
Not an Islay bonfire. Here the smoke sits underneath — a drift of woodsmoke behind the vanilla and lemon, closer to a struck match at the end of the finish than a peat bog. It works well for someone who says they don't like smoky whisky.

Should I add water at 53.4%?
Try it neat first, then add water a few drops at a time. At this strength a little water genuinely changes the whisky — it lifts the citrus and softens the oak. There is no wrong answer, only your preference.

Is this a good gift for a Scotch drinker?
It's one of the best. Anyone deep into Speyside or Highland malts will have heard about the 2026 result and be curious — and few will have bought a bottle for themselves yet. That combination is exactly what makes a gift land.

A Vineyard at the Edge of the Desert
Yatir Winery is founded in the Judean Hills as a joint venture between local growers and Carmel — a small estate with a single ambition: to prove Israel could make a world-class red.
The vineyards sit on the edge of Yatir Forest, Israel's largest planted forest — a green line holding back the Negev desert. The wine is named for it.
At close to 900 metres, days are bright and dry but nights turn genuinely cold. That swing keeps acidity in the grapes and polish in the tannins.
Yatir Forest is the estate's top wine — a Bordeaux-style blend led by Cabernet Sauvignon, aged in oak and released only when it's ready. Kosher throughout.
